sources.entry: T-MAC - Table-lookup kernels for low-bit weights, with a baseline stated but no frequency, compiler or flags, pending those.

summary.one_liner: T-MAC is a kernel library that runs low-bit (int1/2/3/4) mixed-precision matrix multiplication on CPUs using table lookups instead of dequantization, aimed at faster LLM inference on edge devices.
summary.what_it_does: The library computes mixed-precision matmul (int1/2/3/4 weights times int8/fp16/fp32 activations) by precomputing partial sums into lookup tables, using tbl/pshuf instructions on CPUs. It is integrated into a llama.cpp fork for end-to-end inference and supports BitNet (W1.58A8), GPTQ/gguf 4-bit models, and EfficientQAT/BitDistiller 2-bit models. A pipeline script (tools/run_pipeline.py) handles kernel compilation, HF/GPTQ-to-GGUF conversion, and building llama.cpp. The README reports token generation and prefill speedups versus llama.cpp baselines on several devices (Surface Laptop 7, Apple M2-Ultra, Jetson AGX Orin, Raspberry Pi 5), along with power and energy comparisons against an NPU and a CUDA GPU. The README does not state the frequency, compiler, or flags used for the baseline measurements.
use_cases: run low-bit quantized LLMs on a CPU
speed up BitNet b1.58 inference on edge devices
run GPTQ 2-bit or 4-bit models without a GPU
reduce CPU core count and power for local LLM inference
benchmark low-bit mpGEMM kernels against llama.cpp
how_to_run: git clone --recursive <repo> && cd T-MAC && pip install -e . -v && source build/t-mac-envs.sh
stack: conda and Visual Studio on Windows
notable: Table-lookup mpGEMM replaces dequantize-then-multiply, with throughput scaling roughly linearly as bit-width drops
Supports int1/2/3/4 weights with fp16, fp32, or int8 activations
Integrated into llama.cpp for end-to-end inference, including prefill via GEMM kernels
Reports matching llama.cpp throughput with fewer CPU cores (e.g., 2 cores vs 8 on Surface Laptop 7)
Supports GPTQ-format models and a BitNet W1.58A8 path
caveats: The README warns that x86 platforms, especially older generations, may not see speedups, and recommends Surface Book 3 or ARM devices.
Building requires compiling TVM and LLVM from source, which the README says may take a while; Windows needs a multi-step Visual Studio and Clang setup.
Baseline frequency, compiler, and flags for the performance comparisons are not stated; the README notes llama.cpp results vary with the power mode.
keywords: run big model on laptop cpu
